questions.question: State the three household energy needs plus the fourth modern one, describe the energy situation of a typical rural household and a typical informal settlement household, and explain why household energy is a safety and justice issue.
questions.expected_answer: Heating in winter, lighting after dark and cooking including boiling water, plus charging phones and running a radio or television. A rural household in the former homelands often has a grid connection from the post-1994 electrification programme but uses electricity only for lights and a phone because cooking and heating on it is unaffordable, so it cooks and heats on collected wood; an informal settlement household near a city often has no legal connection because the land is unproclaimed or the settlement outgrew the network, so paraffin, candles and illegal connections fill the gap. Roughly one in eight households still cooks mainly on wood, paraffin and candle fires destroy thousands of shacks a year and spread between shacks a metre apart in minutes, so the energy question is about safety and fairness as much as technology.

questions.question: Describe the six energy options available to such households with the main advantage and disadvantage of each, and explain fuel stacking.
questions.expected_answer: Wood is free when gathered and both cooks and heats, but costs hours of collecting, produces harmful indoor smoke, strips the veld and risks burns and fires. Paraffin is cheap per meal, quick and portable, but is poisonous when children drink it from cold-drink bottles, produces fumes, and its stoves tip over and flare, which is why a national stove standard exists. Candles cost a few rand but give too little light to work by and are the most common start of shack fires. LPG in a cylinder cooks fast and clean with good control but needs several hundred rand up front and must be kept outside because a leak indoors can explode. Solar lanterns and small home systems give clean safe light and phone charging for years after a once-off cost but cannot affordably cook or heat. Grid electricity does everything, with Free Basic Electricity covering lights and a radio and prepaid meters allowing small purchases, but cooking and heating on it in winter costs more than many can pay. Fuel stacking is using several sources at once, choosing the cheapest safe-enough option for each task, such as electricity for light, paraffin or gas for cooking, wood for heat and candles when credit runs out.

questions.question: Set out the five criteria for comparing energy options, describe the comparison matrix and what it reveals, and explain why safety campaigns alone fail.
questions.expected_answer: Cost, split into once-off start-up cost and weekly running cost; safety, covering fire, poisoning and shock risk; health, chiefly indoor smoke from wood and paraffin against clean-at-point-of-use gas, solar and electricity, remembering that coal electricity pollutes at the power station; convenience, covering time, carrying and control; and environment, covering vegetation loss, fossil fuel use and coal generation against clean solar. A matrix with options across the top and criteria down the side, scored or described in each cell, shows that no option is best on every row, that the most dangerous options are the cheapest to start, and that the safest options need lump sums poor households lack. Telling a family not to use a candle does not light their room, so real solutions change the economics through cheaper solar lanterns, subsidised gas, more Free Basic Electricity, legal connections and safer standard-compliant stoves.
